newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans mourn victims of Frankfurt Christmas attack.
newsitem.headline: Germans mourn victims of Frankfurt Christmas attack.

text.p: More than 800 mourners packed a Frankfurt church on Sunday evening for a special memorial service for victims of Christmas Eve suicide grenade attack that killed three and left Germany horrified.

Saying prayers for the three women killed and 13 injured, local church and political leaders spoke of the lingering shock and pain that filled the city five days after a 49-year-old woman detonated two hand grenades strapped to her body.
The blast during a midnight church service on Christmas Eve blew the Frankfurt woman to pieces and killed two elderly sisters sitting in front of her.
The 13 injured, who included a 12-year-old girl, were caught in a wave of shrapnel and splinters of pews shattered by the blast.

"The detonation and its horrible aftermath abruptly ended the silence of the holy night," Frankfurt mayor Petra Roth told the crowded service in a Catholic church only a few hundred metres (yards) away from the scene of the crime.

"We send out our heartfelt sympathies to the victims of this," she added. "We also have to ask ourselves: should we not offer more spiritual warmth to our fellow human beings before our souls freeze over."

German police said the 49-year-old woman, Heidrun-Erika J., who killed herself and two other women, had been haunted by the suicide of her 18-year-old son seven years ago. She had been in psychiatric care ever since her son threw himself under a train near the church in 1989.

Police identified the two grenades that killed the three women and injured 13 other worshippers as M-52 models, believed made in Yugoslavia. Police were focusing their investigation on how the woman had obtained the grenades.
Hans Blum, the pastor of the Protestant church, was holding one of his final services before retiring. He was leading the 70 worshippers in singing Christmas carols when the blast went off.
"We saw death and violence so close to us that it has taken our breath away," Blum said.
Among those who attended the church service, which was broadcast on local television, was the state of Hesse's justice minister, Rupert von Plottnitz, and the state church president Peter Steinacker.
"We have to ask ourselves how all this could happen," Steinacker said. "The images of horror and fear will not go away."
Most of those hurt were no longer in critical condition, but authorities said it was still uncertain whether the mother of the 12-year-old girl, a church worker, would survive.
Police said the suicide bomber had been separated from her husband and nine-year-old daughter.
After her son's death seven years ago, the woman moved with her husband and young daughter to another Frankfurt district. She then moved by herself to the outlying town of Usingen in October 1995.
